# Agent Stacks

> An open specification for an agent's parts on disk: the harness, its plugins, and the
> runtimes both need, as one unit that runs the same way on every machine. Specification
> 0.1.0 is a draft and will change.

An agent is composed of many parts. Top to bottom: the model, its plugins, the harness, the
commands the harness can run, the sandbox that provides them, and the secrets the agent may
use. No two agents have all of the same parts, so behavior differs from user to user.

Agent Stacks is an open specification for shipping all of these parts as one unit.

## What problem does this solve?

Imagine that you use the caveman plugin. Its compression skill requires Python 3.10 or newer.
However, your machine has Python 3.9.6, so the skill fails when the agent runs it.

Most agents are managed like this, as bespoke snowflakes. In contrast, an agent stack defines
all of the parts in code so they run the same everywhere.

## Try a reference implementation

Nix reference implementation:

    nix run github:agent-stacks/claude-code

Needs Nix with flakes. Compatible with x86_64-linux, aarch64-linux, aarch64-darwin. Intel Mac
is not supported. You do not need the agent, Python, or Agent Stacks installed first.

The command above puts one directory on your machine with all of the parts, then launches
the agent stack.

    agent-stack-claude-code/
    ├── bin/claude-code       # the launcher for the stack
    └── share/agent-plugins/
        ├── caveman/          # plugin
        │   ├── plugin.json
        │   ├── skills/caveman-compress/scripts/compress.py
        │   └── bin/python3   # the runtime for compress.py
        └── agentmemory/      # plugin
            ├── plugin.json
            ├── mcp.json
            ├── skills/
            └── bin/npx       # the runtime for mcp.json's command

## Where to start

- I use a harness every day. You can use Agent Stacks to manage the configuration of your
  existing harness (Claude Code, Codex, Pi). Developer quick start:
  https://github.com/agent-stacks/agent-pkgs#quick-start
- I manage agents for a team. You can use Agent Stacks to define the harness and plugins for
  a team and keep them current. Create an agent stack:
  https://github.com/agent-stacks/agent-pkgs/blob/main/docs/guides/create-agent-stack.md
- I write skills or MCP servers. You can use Agent Stacks to package skills or MCP servers
  together with their dependencies, so they run the same everywhere. Create an agent plugin:
  https://github.com/agent-stacks/agent-pkgs/blob/main/docs/guides/create-agent-plugin.md

## What's on the roadmap?

The Agent Stacks stack is in active development. It currently supports plugins, harnesses,
and commands, with new features coming soon.

- Model: local models and model routing. Planned.
- Plugins: skills and MCP servers. Today.
- Plugins: hooks, rules, and subagents. In progress.
- Harness: claude, codex, opencode, pi, agent-deck. Today.
- Commands: interpreters such as python3 and npx. Today. The specification calls these
  runtimes.
- Sandbox: what the agent can reach. In progress.
- Secrets: credentials the agent may use. Planned.

We are looking for contributors, especially for native support in more package managers and
more harnesses. See "Open development" below for how to get involved.

## What the specification says

The website no longer summarizes the specification. This section is kept here for reference.

It defines no requirements of its own. Every MUST comes from one of the three specifications
it composes: Agent Plugins (the plugin package), Agent Skills (what a skill is), and MCP (how
a plugin's servers behave on the wire). On top of those it recommends:

- A stack is one directory.
- It has exactly one harness and any number of plugins. To run two harnesses, build two
  stacks.
- Each plugin gets its own directory at share/agent-plugins/<name>/.
- There is one launcher, at bin/<stack-name>.
- The layout is harness-neutral. The launcher adapts it to the harness every time it runs.
- A stack is transportable as one unit. Copy it with its dependencies to a machine that has
  none of its runtimes installed, and it still runs. The specification calls this the point
  of the whole document.

A stack decides what the agent brings with it, and has no say over what the agent reaches
once it is running. The launcher puts the stack's harness first on PATH and leaves the rest
alone, so an agent that runs git gets the host's git.

The build finds a runtime only in a script's shebang or an MCP server's command. A SKILL.md
that tells the agent to run rg still depends on the host's rg.

A stack is explicitly NOT a sandbox, NOT a package manager, and NOT a per-harness
configuration tree. There is no stack-level manifest, so the spec version a stack was built
against is not discoverable on disk.

## Vocabulary

The website says "harness". The specification says "agent client", a term from Agent Plugins.
They mean the same thing, and the specification lets an implementation use whichever name
its users know.

## Current numbers

- 307 plugin packages in agent-pkgs.
- 5 harnesses can be a stack's harness today: agent-deck, claude, codex, opencode, pi.
- ~170 agent CLIs are packaged by numtide/llm-agents.nix, of which 56 are classified as
  agents. Do not confuse that catalogue with the five that work as a stack harness.

## Open development

Agent Stacks is developed in public. Flox is the initial sponsor and wrote the first
implementation, and we are looking for contributors and collaborators. We are not attached to
any particular technology. The specification is a layout on disk; Nix is just one way to
produce it.

If you are packaging agent tooling already, or you maintain a harness that has to load
components, we are open to collaborating: https://go.flox.dev/slack
